sysdesign.outcome: On launch Monday the system handled a measured peak of 22 requests per second with a p95 response time of 4.1 seconds and an error rate under 0.5 percent. The cache answered 37 percent of questions, which cut the model bill for the week by about a third compared with the estimate without caching.
lessons: Start with a back-of-envelope load estimate; it turns 'will it hold?' into numbers you can defend.
Stateless app servers plus shared state in Redis and a database let you add servers without surprises.
Plan what happens when each part fails, especially the external AI provider.
Say out loud what you chose not to build and why.
discuss: What would change if the assistant had to answer from documents that differ by country and user permissions?
When would you add a queue to this design, and what user experience would it create?
The cache answers 37 percent of questions. How would you stop it from serving an answer after the underlying policy document changes?

warehouse.title: Quorrin Market: why the AI forecast and finance never agreed on revenue
warehouse.company: Quorrin Market (made up), supermarket chain, 120 stores, Australia
warehouse.situation: An FDE was deploying a demand forecasting model that wrote weekly predictions per store and category. In the first review, the model's 'actual revenue' for last quarter was 3.8 percent higher than the finance dashboard, and the CFO stopped the meeting to ask which number was wrong. Category managers for 14 departments were waiting to use the forecasts for ordering.
warehouse.problem: The model's training data had been pulled straight from the point-of-sale database with a hand-written query, while finance used the warehouse's dbt models, which removed refunds and staff discounts and mapped stores to their current regions. Patching the forecast query to 'look like' finance would have created a second, silently diverging definition of revenue.
approach: Read the customer's dbt project and lineage graph to find the model finance used: fct_sales joined to dim_store, dim_product and dim_date in a star schema.
Reconciled one store for one week line by line and found the gap: refunds and staff discounts kept in the raw query, plus 2 stores moved between regions.
Pointed the forecast pipeline at fct_sales instead of the POS database, so the model and finance shared one definition of revenue.
Added a new dbt model, fct_forecast, at the same grain (store, category, week) with foreign keys to the same dimensions, so forecasts and actuals could be joined in one query.
Added dbt tests for not-null keys, unique grain and relationships to the dimensions, and a custom test that fails if weekly totals drift more than 0.5 percent from finance's revenue.
Documented the new model in the dbt project so it appeared in the lineage graph next to the finance models.

artifact.code:
-- models/marts/fct_forecast_vs_actual.sql
{{ config(materialized='table') }}

select
    f.store_key,
    f.category_key,
    f.week_key,
    f.predicted_revenue,
    coalesce(sum(s.net_revenue), 0) as actual_revenue,
    f.predicted_revenue - coalesce(sum(s.net_revenue), 0) as error
from {{ ref('fct_forecast') }} f
left join {{ ref('fct_sales') }} s
    on  s.store_key    = f.store_key
    and s.category_key = f.category_key
    and s.week_key     = f.week_key
group by 1, 2, 3, 4

warehouse.outcome: After the switch, the model's actual revenue matched the finance dashboard to within 0.1 percent for every week of the quarter. Forecast error measured against the trusted actuals was 6.2 percent at store and category level, and the CFO approved use by all 14 category teams.
lessons: Build on the customer's trusted warehouse models instead of re-deriving business numbers from raw tables.
Match the grain and reuse the same dimensions so new AI outputs join cleanly to existing facts.
dbt tests turn 'the numbers look right' into checks that run every night.
When two numbers disagree, reconcile one small slice by hand before changing any code.
discuss: Who should own fct_forecast after the FDE leaves, the data team or the forecasting team?
How would you handle a store that changes region mid-quarter when comparing forecasts over time?
The forecasting team needs a field that the finance dbt models do not have yet. How would you add it without creating a second version of revenue?

dsa.title: Zelvora Payments: the duplicate-merchant script that would have run for a week
dsa.company: Zelvora Payments (made up), payment processing, about 300 staff, Netherlands
dsa.situation: Before loading merchant records into a new AI risk-scoring tool, an FDE had to find likely duplicates among 1.2 million merchants from three onboarding systems. A customer analyst's script compared every merchant with every other one and had handled a 5,000-row sample in 12 seconds. On the full table it was projected to take more than a week.
dsa.problem: The script was O(n squared): 1.2 million records means about 720 billion pairs. A bigger machine or parallel workers would divide that by 8 or 16, but still leave a day or more of runtime and no room to rerun after fixing a rule.
approach: Estimated the cost out loud from the sample: 5,000 rows is 12.5 million pairs in 12 seconds, about a million pairs a second, so 720 billion pairs is roughly 720,000 seconds, or 8 days, on one core.
Replaced the pairwise loop with a hash map keyed on a normalized form of each merchant: VAT number where present, otherwise cleaned name plus postcode.
Grouped records by key in one O(n) pass, so only records sharing a key were compared in detail.
For near-miss names, used blocking: bucket by postcode, then compare names only within each bucket, which kept the expensive comparisons small.
Used a heap to keep the 200 largest duplicate groups for manual review by the operations team.
Tested the new script on the 5,000-row sample and confirmed it found the same duplicate pairs as the original.
dsa.outcome: The full 1.2 million records ran in 3 minutes 40 seconds instead of a projected 8 days. It found about 41,000 duplicate groups; the operations team confirmed 96 percent of a 300-group random sample as real duplicates, and the risk tool launched with a clean merchant table a week earlier than planned.
lessons: Always check how an approach grows before running it on the customer's full data.
When you see a loop inside a loop searching for matches, ask whether a dict keyed on the right value removes the inner loop.
Blocking (only comparing within small buckets) makes fuzzy matching affordable.
Keep the slow, obviously correct version as a test for the fast one.
discuss: What duplicates would the normalized key miss, and how would you find them without going back to O(n squared)?
If the table grew to 50 million rows, what would you change?
How would you test the normalized-key approach so the operations team trusts that it does not merge merchants that are genuinely different?

discovery.title: Marrowline Water: the 'chatbot' request that turned out to be a search problem
discovery.company: Marrowline Water (made up), regional water utility, about 1,100 staff, United States
discovery.situation: Marrowline's customer service director asked for 'an AI chatbot on our website' to cut call volume. The contact center of 45 agents handled about 1,300 calls a day, with an average handling time of 7.5 minutes and a backlog that peaked after every billing run.
discovery.problem: Nobody had checked why customers were calling or where the time went. Building the chatbot straight away risked a polished tool that answered questions customers were not asking, while agents kept struggling with the real bottleneck.
approach: Wrote an interview guide with one goal (find where call time goes and why) and open, past-behavior questions such as 'walk me through the last call that took more than 10 minutes'.
Interviewed 6 agents, 2 team leads and the billing supervisor for 45 minutes each, asking 'why' until answers reached something concrete.
Shadowed four agents for a morning and timed each call step, noting every screen they opened.

Tagged 400 recent call notes by reason and found that 38 percent were about estimated bills and meter readings, and that on those calls agents spent about half the time searching three old knowledge bases and a shared drive.
Wrote a one-paragraph problem statement with the baseline and a success measure, and got the director and two team leads to agree to it in writing.
Proposed starting with an agent-facing answer search over the knowledge bases, with the public chatbot as a later phase once answers were trusted.

          agents spend about half of each call searching three old

Ask about the last real time something happened, then watch people work; stories and timings beat opinions.
End discovery with a written problem statement that has a baseline number and a success measure.
A narrower first phase that fixes the real bottleneck often makes the original request succeed later.
discuss: How would you handle the director if they insisted on the public chatbot first?
What would you do if agents and team leads described the problem very differently?
What would you measure in the first two weeks after launch to confirm the search tool is solving the problem you found in discovery?

docs.title: Talwyn Cooperative Bank: the SOW that promised 'all product documents'
docs.company: Talwyn Cooperative Bank (made up), retail bank, about 2,200 staff and 60 branches, Wales
docs.situation: Talwyn signed a 10-week engagement for an assistant that helps branch staff answer product questions. Three weeks in, the branch operations manager expected mortgage, savings and insurance documents, the FDE team had only planned for savings and current accounts, and the bank's security architect had not yet seen how customer data would flow.

Wrote a design doc covering architecture, data flow, where documents and logs are stored, access control through the bank's existing single sign-on, and a no-customer-data rule for phase 1.
Sent the design doc to the security architect for a review meeting in week 4 instead of week 9.
Started a decision log and recorded each choice, starting with 'Insurance products moved to phase 2 because they need compliance review'.

How would you raise the SOW ambiguity without making the account lead or the customer feel blamed?
Which parts of the design doc would you keep up to date after launch, and which would you let freeze as a record of what was decided?

demo.title: Ambervane Health Cover: a demo that survived the conference-room Wi-Fi
demo.company: Ambervane Health Cover (made up), health insurer, about 1,600 staff, Canada
demo.situation: After a four-week pilot of an assistant that summarizes pre-authorization requests, the FDE had 30 minutes with the VP of operations, the medical director and the CFO to win approval for a rollout to 90 reviewers. The previous vendor's demo had been a 25-screen feature tour that ended with the CFO asking 'so what does this save us?'.
demo.problem: The assistant had many features (summaries, policy lookups, draft letters, a dashboard), and the temptation was to show them all. The live demo also depended on the customer's guest Wi-Fi and a model API, either of which could fail in the room.
approach: Built the story around one reviewer from discovery, called Dana in the demo, and one real type of request: an MRI pre-authorization, using a de-identified case approved by privacy.
Opened with the before: a 40-second screen recording of Dana moving through five screens, and the measured baseline of 17 minutes per request.
Showed the after live on the same case: the summary, the matching policy clause with a citation, and a draft decision letter, reaching the key moment within the first 8 minutes.
Prepared a fallback: a recorded run of the same case and screenshots, plus a phone hotspot, and rehearsed switching to them calmly.
Closed with pilot numbers, an honest note on two cases where the summary missed a detail, and one clear ask: approve a 90-reviewer rollout starting next month.

demo.outcome: The Wi-Fi dropped in minute 9, and the FDE switched to the recording in about 20 seconds without losing the thread. The rollout was approved in the meeting based on pilot results of 17 down to 7 minutes per request, and the CFO asked for the run sheet to reuse in the board update.
lessons: Tell one named user's story with one workflow; skip features that do not serve it.
Show the painful before with a real number, then the same task after.
Assume the live step can fail and rehearse the switch to a backup.
End with a specific ask, and mention the limits yourself before someone else does.
discuss: How would you change this demo for an audience of reviewers instead of executives?
Is it ever right to show only a recording and no live demo?
The pilot numbers were 17 minutes down to 7. How would you present them so a sceptical finance director trusts them?

builddrill.title: Meera's 90-minute build: shipping a thin slice instead of a half-built LLM pipeline
builddrill.company: Meera (made up), data engineer with 6 years' experience, interviewing for an FDE role at Lumquist (made up), a 400-person AI software company, Singapore
builddrill.situation: Meera received a live 90-minute build prompt: build a small service that takes a support ticket and returns a category and a confidence, using a provided CSV of 2,000 labeled tickets. In a practice run the week before, she had spent 70 minutes wiring up an LLM call and a vector store and ended with nothing that ran and no tests.
builddrill.problem: The prompt invited an ambitious AI solution, but reviewers score clarifying questions, a working core path, tests and honest trade-offs. Trying the fancy approach first risked the same result as the practice run: impressive plans and no working service.
approach: Spent the first 10 minutes reading and asking three clarifying questions: expected volume, whether an LLM API key was allowed, and whether a simple baseline counted.
Wrote a time plan in the README: scaffold by minute 25, core path by 55, tests by 70, README and cuts by 85.
Built the core path with FastAPI and a Pydantic request model, using a keyword and TF-IDF baseline trained on the CSV, so an end-to-end request worked by minute 50.
Wrote tests for the happy path, an empty ticket (422) and a ticket with no known words (returns 'other' with low confidence).
At minute 70, decided not to add the LLM call and wrote the trade-off in the README instead: how she would add it behind the same interface and evaluate it against the baseline's 79 percent accuracy.
Used the last 10 minutes to run everything from a clean terminal and walk the interviewer through the design and the cuts.

artifact.code:
# tests/test_triage.py
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from app.main import app

client = TestClient(app)

def test_billing_ticket_is_classified():
    r = client.post("/triage", json={"text": "I was charged twice for my invoice"})
    assert r.status_code == 200
    body = r.json()
    assert body["category"] == "billing"
    assert 0.0 <= body["confidence"] <= 1.0

def test_empty_ticket_is_rejected():
    r = client.post("/triage", json={"text": ""})
    assert r.status_code == 422

def test_unknown_words_fall_back_to_other():
    r = client.post("/triage", json={"text": "zxqv plorth"})
    assert r.json()["category"] == "other"
    assert r.json()["confidence"] < 0.5

builddrill.outcome: Meera finished with a running service, 3 passing tests and a README listing two cuts and how she would address them, with 4 minutes to spare. The interviewer's feedback noted her clarifying questions and her decision at minute 70 as strengths, and she advanced to the final round.
lessons: Clarify first; three good questions in the first 10 minutes save half an hour later.
A simple baseline that works end to end beats an ambitious pipeline that does not run.
Cut scope, not tests or the README, and write down what you cut and why.
Check the clock at planned points so you notice a rabbit hole early.
discuss: If the interviewer said 'we really want to see an LLM used', how would you change the plan?
What is the smallest set of tests that still shows good judgment in 90 minutes?
With 20 minutes left, one test fails and the README is unwritten. Which do you fix first, and how do you explain the choice to the interviewer?

career.title: Arjun's resume rewrite: from 'responsible for pipelines' to FDE interviews

career.situation: Arjun applied to 30 FDE and solutions engineering roles over two months and got 1 recruiter call. Practiced each story out loud to a 2-minute limit, recording himself and cutting background until the Action and Result took most of the time.

apistyles.title: Tremholt Freight: replacing a minute-by-minute poll with carrier webhooks
apistyles.company: Tremholt Freight (made up), freight forwarder, 650 staff, Germany
apistyles.situation: Tremholt's customer portal showed shipment status by polling three partner carriers' REST APIs every minute for about 5,000 open shipments. The busiest carrier started returning 429 errors most afternoons, and customer service logged around 120 calls a week from customers whose portal status was hours out of date.
apistyles.problem: Polling faster or buying a higher API tier would raise cost and still waste over 95 percent of calls on shipments that had not changed. Two of the three carriers offered signed webhooks, but Tremholt had never run a public endpoint and worried about fake or duplicate events.
approach: Read each carrier's OpenAPI spec and webhook documentation, listing event types, payload fields and the signature scheme (HMAC SHA-256 over the raw body).
Built a small FastAPI receiver that verifies the signature, rejects bad calls with 401, stores the raw event, puts it on a queue and returns 200 within about 50 ms.
Made processing idempotent by keying on the carrier's event id, so retries and duplicates changed nothing, and ignored events older than the latest status already stored.
Kept polling only for the third carrier and slowed it to every 10 minutes, and added an hourly reconciliation poll for any shipment with no update in 24 hours.
Wrapped Tremholt's own status data in a versioned /v1 REST API with an OpenAPI spec, so the portal and two large customers' systems read from one contract.

artifact.code:
@app.post("/webhooks/{carrier}")
async def receive(carrier: str, request: Request):
    raw = await request.body()
    secret = SECRETS[carrier]                         # one secret per carrier
    expected = hmac.new(secret, raw, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(request.headers.get("X-Signature", ""), expected):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
    event = json.loads(raw)
    inserted = db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO carrier_events (carrier, event_id, body) VALUES (%s, %s, %s) "
        "ON CONFLICT (carrier, event_id) DO NOTHING",
        (carrier, event["id"], raw.decode()),
    ).rowcount
    if inserted:
        queue.send({"carrier": carrier, "event_id": event["id"]})
    return {"ok": True}                               # fast 200 so they stop retrying

apistyles.outcome: Calls to the two webhook carriers fell from about 430,000 a day to about 9,000 events plus the hourly reconciliation, and the 429 errors stopped. Median delay between a carrier scan and the portal update went from 11 minutes to under 1 minute, and 'status is out of date' calls dropped from about 120 to about 35 a week.
lessons: Webhooks give fresher data with far fewer calls, but only with signature checks, fast replies and idempotent handling.
Keep a slow reconciliation poll as a safety net for events missed during outages.
Publishing your own API with an OpenAPI spec and a version number lets several consumers share one contract.
discuss: What would you do if a carrier's webhook endpoint went silent for three hours without any errors?
When would you choose to keep polling even though webhooks are available?
The third carrier only offers polling. How would you design the system so adding its webhooks later changes as little code as possible?

nosql.title: Quellora Home: talking a retailer out of a full database migration
nosql.company: Quellora Home (made up), online furniture retailer, 220 staff, Portugal
nosql.situation: Quellora's leadership asked the FDE team to move everything from Postgres to MongoDB because product pages were slow and a new AI 'find similar items' feature was planned. Product pages had a median load time of 1.8 seconds, and the catalog held 38,000 products with very different attributes per category.
nosql.problem: A full migration would take months and break finance's SQL reports, which join orders, payments and refunds. The slowness had not been measured, so there was no evidence that a different database would fix it.
approach: Listed the eight most important reads and writes with volumes, including product page loads (about 60 per second at peak), checkout transactions and monthly finance reports.
Profiled the product page and found it ran 14 queries against an attribute table with one row per attribute, so a single product needed dozens of rows joined back together.
Moved variable attributes into a JSONB column with a GIN index, so each product page reads one row, while orders and payments stayed relational with their transactions and joins.
Moved user sessions and carts from Postgres to Redis with a 30-minute expiry, removing about 40 percent of write traffic from the main database.
Added pgvector to the products table for 'similar items', storing one embedding per product and filtering by in-stock status in the same SQL query.
Wrote a one-page decision table for leadership showing each access pattern, the chosen store and why MongoDB was not needed now.

artifact.code:
ACCESS PATTERN                  VOLUME        STORE              WHY
Product page by id              60/s peak     Postgres + JSONB   one row, flexible attrs
Filter by attribute             10/s          Postgres GIN index JSON containment queries
Checkout (order + payment)      2/s           Postgres           needs a transaction
Sessions and carts              300/s         Redis, TTL 30 min  key lookups, short-lived
Similar items                   15/s          pgvector (HNSW)    filter by stock in SQL
Finance monthly reports         monthly       Postgres replica   joins, ad hoc SQL

System of record: Postgres. Redis data can be lost without harm.
Revisit MongoDB only if catalog writes exceed what one Postgres primary handles.

nosql.outcome: Median product page load fell from 1.8 seconds to 0.4 seconds and database CPU at peak dropped from about 75 percent to 40 percent. The similar-items feature shipped in five weeks on pgvector, and finance reports kept working with no migration project.
lessons: Measure the slow path before choosing a new database; the cause is often a query or schema problem.
Postgres with JSONB and pgvector covers many document and vector needs with one system to run.
Use specialized stores such as Redis for data whose access pattern clearly fits, and keep one system of record.
discuss: What evidence would make you recommend a move to a document database after all?
How would you explain to a non-technical executive why their preferred database was not chosen?
If the product catalogue grew to 50 million items with very different attributes per category, which parts would you reconsider, and why?

streaming.title: Varnbrook Mutual: moving card fraud checks from nightly batch to streaming
streaming.company: Varnbrook Mutual (made up), building society with card accounts, 1,900 staff, United Kingdom
streaming.situation: Varnbrook ran its fraud rules as a nightly batch job over the day's card transactions. Fraud was often spotted 12 to 30 hours after the first bad payment, by which time a compromised card had typically made several more purchases. Losses from card fraud averaged about 38,000 pounds a month.
streaming.problem: Running the batch every hour would still leave a gap of up to an hour and would hammer the core banking database with repeated scans. The core system was vendor software, so its code could not be changed to publish events.
approach: Agreed with the DBA to enable logical replication on the transactions database and create a dedicated replication user, then deployed Debezium to stream inserts from two tables into Kafka.
Created the topic with 12 partitions keyed by card id, so every transaction for one card stays in order in one partition.
Wrote the fraud scorer as a consumer group of four instances, keeping per-card state for a 10-minute window: count of payments, distinct merchant countries and total amount.
Used at-least-once delivery with offsets committed after processing, and wrote alerts with an upsert keyed by transaction id so reprocessing could never create duplicate alerts.
Added dashboards and alerts for consumer lag and for the database's retained replication log size, with a runbook for a stuck connector.
Kept the nightly batch running in parallel for four weeks and compared its alerts to the streaming alerts before switching the batch off.

artifact.code:
WINDOW = timedelta(minutes=10)
recent = defaultdict(deque)          # card_id -> deque of (time, amount, country)

def score(tx):
    q = recent[tx["card_id"]]
    now = tx["ts"]
    q.append((now, tx["amount"], tx["country"]))
    while q and now - q[0][0] > WINDOW:  # drop events outside the window
        q.popleft()
    countries = {c for _, _, c in q}
    total = sum(a for _, a, _ in q)
    if len(q) >= 6 or len(countries) >= 3 or total > 3000:
        upsert_alert(tx["tx_id"], reason=f"{len(q)} tx, {len(countries)} countries")

while True:
    msg = consumer.poll(1.0)
    if msg is None or msg.error():
        continue
    score(parse_debezium(msg.value()))
    consumer.commit(message=msg)       # commit after the alert is safely written

streaming.outcome: Median time from first suspicious payment to alert fell from about 18 hours to 40 seconds. Over the first three months card fraud losses averaged about 24,000 pounds a month, roughly 37 percent lower, and the core database showed no measurable extra load.
lessons: Log-based CDC gets events out of systems you cannot modify, without polling their tables.
Choose the partition key for the ordering you need; here all events for one card must stay in order.
At-least-once with idempotent writes is a practical, robust default for writing to outside systems.
Run the old batch in parallel before switching, so you can prove the new pipeline is complete.
discuss: In-memory state is lost if a consumer restarts. How would you rebuild or persist the 10-minute window?
Which fraud checks would you still leave in a nightly batch, and why?
On a busy sale day one consumer falls 20 minutes behind. What does that mean for fraud detection, and what would you do about it?

cicd.title: Olvenmark Health Analytics: from SSH deploys to a gated pipeline
cicd.company: Olvenmark Health Analytics (made up), hospital analytics software vendor, 90 staff, Sweden
cicd.situation: Olvenmark's FDE team maintained a patient-flow prediction service for three hospital regions. Deploys meant SSH-ing into a server and running git pull and a restart, about once a week. In one quarter two deploys broke production, one for 3 hours, and a regional hospital's IT security team paused further releases until changes were controlled.
cicd.problem: Asking engineers to 'be more careful' would not satisfy the hospital's change control, which required evidence of testing, scanning and a named approver for each release. Deploying less often would make each release bigger and riskier.
approach: Added a GitHub Actions workflow that runs ruff, unit tests and integration tests against a Postgres service container on every pull request, and required it to pass before merging.
Added dependency scanning with pip-audit and image scanning with Trivy, failing the build on critical vulnerabilities.
Built the Docker image once on merge to main, tagged it with the commit SHA and deployed that same image to staging automatically.
Created a production environment in GitHub with two required reviewers from the hospital-facing team and switched cloud access to short-lived OIDC credentials, removing stored keys.
Put a new model version behind a feature flag, enabled first for one hospital's two wards, so model changes could be turned off in seconds.
Wrote and rehearsed a rollback script that redeploys the previous image tag and runs a health check.

integration.situation: Corvastro wanted an AI demand forecast to cut stockouts of spare parts, which caused about 9 percent of service orders to be delayed. integration.problem: Corvastro's IT roadmap promised a modern API platform in 18 months, and the pilot had 12 weeks. Direct access to SAP's production database was not allowed, and one early script using a manager's Salesforce login broke when the manager changed his password.

Extended Corvastro's existing MuleSoft flow, owned by IT, to export SAP sales orders and material master data to a staging schema every 30 minutes, instead of building a new SAP connection.
Took distributor purchase orders already parsed by Corvastro's EDI translator from its output tables, and mapped distributor part codes to Corvastro part numbers with a maintained lookup table.
Built an SFTP pickup job for the warehouse inventory file that waits for a .done marker, checks the trailer row count and records file checksums to skip repeats.
Replaced the personal Salesforce login with a service account limited to reading Cases and Assets, stored its credentials in the customer's vault, and used backoff on 429 responses.
Added monitoring for late files, failed loads and daily API quota use, with alerts to both the FDE team and the owning Corvastro team.

bi.title: Tallowfen Physio: one definition of an active patient
bi.company: Tallowfen Physio (made up), physiotherapy clinic chain, 40 clinics and 600 staff, Canada
bi.situation: Tallowfen had deployed an AI scheduling assistant and needed to show whether it improved clinic utilization. The company had 14 Power BI dashboards, and three of them reported 'active patients' as 11,200, 13,900 and 16,400 for the same month. Leadership meetings spent more time arguing about numbers than acting on them.
bi.problem: Building yet another dashboard for the AI pilot would add a fourth number. The disagreement came from different definitions in each report's SQL, not from the tool, so the fix had to happen in the data model and the metric definitions.
approach: Collected the SQL behind each 'active patient' figure and found three definitions: any booking in 90 days, any attended visit in 90 days, and any record not marked discharged.
Ran a 45-minute session with the clinical operations director and finance, who agreed: a patient with at least one attended visit in the last 60 days, excluding cancelled and no-show visits.
Built modeled tables in the warehouse, fct_visits and a daily summary agg_clinic_daily, and encoded active patients and utilization once in the Power BI data model with written descriptions.
Designed one pilot dashboard with four KPI tiles (utilization, active patients, no-show rate, AI-booked share), a 16-week trend, a bar chart by clinic and a detail table, and showed the refresh time.
Reconciled the headline visit count against the billing system for two months before launch, and repointed the three existing dashboards to the shared definitions.

artifact.code:
-- Agreed definition, signed off by clinical ops and finance
-- Active patient: >= 1 attended visit in the 60 days up to the report date
WITH attended AS (
    SELECT patient_id, clinic_id, visit_date
    FROM fct_visits
    WHERE status = 'attended'              -- excludes cancelled, no_show
)
SELECT d.report_date,
       count(DISTINCT a.patient_id) AS active_patients
FROM dim_date d
JOIN attended a
  ON a.visit_date >  d.report_date - 60
 AND a.visit_date <= d.report_date
WHERE d.is_month_end                    -- one row per month
  AND d.report_date >= current_date - interval '12 months'
GROUP BY d.report_date
ORDER BY d.report_date;

bi.outcome: All dashboards now show one active patient figure, 12,650 for the reference month, and the pilot dashboard loads in about 2 seconds instead of 40. Over 16 weeks, pilot clinics' utilization rose from 71 to 77 percent against 72 to 73 percent in comparison clinics, a result leadership accepted without dispute.
lessons: Conflicting numbers are usually conflicting definitions; fix them with the business owners before touching charts.
Define each metric once, in a metrics layer or shared model, and point every dashboard at it.
A dashboard that proves AI impact needs a baseline and a comparison group, not just a current value.
discuss: Clinical operations and finance cannot agree on a definition. How would you move forward?
Which of the four KPI tiles would you remove if the dashboard had room for only three, and why?
A clinic manager exports the dashboard to Excel and adds their own filters, producing a different number again. How would you respond?

dimred.title: Veldmark Mutual: a ticket map that almost created five fake customer segments
dimred.company: Veldmark Mutual (made up), home and motor insurer, about 1,200 staff, Netherlands
dimred.situation: Veldmark's customer-service team had embedded 180,000 support tickets with a text embedding model (1,536 numbers each) and a consultant had shown the board a UMAP map with five colourful blobs. The board wanted five new service teams, one per blob, and asked the FDE to 'productionise the segments'. Ticket routing was manual and took a median of 9 hours.
dimred.problem: Nobody had checked whether the five blobs were real groups or an artefact of the map settings, and the blob sizes on the slide were being read as team sizes. Building five teams from the picture could lock in a structure that did not match the tickets.
approach: Reran UMAP with three n_neighbors values and three seeds; the map showed between four and eight blobs, and their relative sizes changed each time.
Reduced the embeddings with PCA to 50 components (keeping 82 percent of the variance) to make later steps fast and stable, fitting PCA on a training sample only.
Ran k-means clustering on the 50 PCA components for k from 3 to 12 and compared silhouette scores and stability across resamples (see clustering); seven groups were the most stable.
Read 30 tickets from each group with two senior agents, who named six clear topics and one mixed group of 'other'.
Used the map only as a navigation aid in the review tool, with a caption explaining what it can and cannot show.
Trained a simple classifier on the PCA components to route new tickets to the six named topics, with low-confidence tickets going to a general queue.

artifact.code:
How to read the ticket map (caption shown on the dashboard)

Each dot is one support ticket. Tickets about similar things sit near each other.

You CAN use this map to:
- browse examples of a topic and find tickets that look misfiled
- see whether a new batch of tickets lands in familiar areas

You CANNOT use this map to:
- count topics (the number of blobs changes with settings)
- compare topic sizes (blob size is not ticket volume)
- compare how different two topics are (gaps are not distances)

Topic counts and sizes come from the routing report, not from this picture.
Questions: analytics team, #ticket-routing

dimred.outcome: The board approved six topic queues instead of five new teams, re-using existing staff. Median time to the right queue fell from 9 hours to under 2, and misrouted tickets, measured by reassignment, dropped from 21 percent to 12 percent over the first two months.
lessons: A t-SNE or UMAP map is a way to ask questions, never evidence for how many groups exist or how big they are.
PCA to a few dozen components is a sensible, fast step before clustering or classifying large embeddings.
Human reading of samples from each group is what turns clusters into names people trust.
Put the reading rules next to the picture, because the picture will be screenshotted and forwarded.
discuss: How would you explain to a board member, in two sentences, why the blob sizes on the slide were misleading?
What would you monitor to notice that new ticket types are appearing that fit none of the six topics?
If the six topic queues turn out to be uneven, with one getting half of all tickets, would you split it, and what evidence would you use?

anomaly.title: Orvella Payments: from 900 daily fraud alerts to 60 that analysts trust
anomaly.company: Orvella Payments (made up), card payments processor for about 3,000 small merchants, Portugal
anomaly.situation: Orvella's in-house rule engine raised about 900 fraud alerts a day for a team of four analysts who could review roughly 60. Analysts had started bulk-closing alerts, and confirmed fraud losses were about 38,000 euros a month. There were only 140 confirmed fraud cases in the last year.
anomaly.problem: Every rule used a fixed global threshold (any payment over 3 standard deviations of all merchants' amounts), which flagged big but normal merchants all day and missed small merchants being abused at night. With so few labels, a supervised fraud model was not yet realistic.
approach: Sorted the known cases with the fraud lead into point (single huge refunds), contextual (odd hour or country for that merchant) and collective (bursts of tiny card-testing payments) patterns.
Replaced global thresholds with per-merchant robust baselines: median and IQR of amount by merchant and hour of day, scoring each payment's deviation from its own context.

Added an isolation forest over eight features (amount versus merchant median, hour, card age, country mismatch, payments per card in 10 minutes and so on) and blended its score with the robust scores.
Set the alert count from the review budget: the top 60 scores per day, with collective bursts grouped into one alert per card.
Built a simple review form so every alert got a label and a reason, and sampled 20 unflagged payments a week to estimate misses.
Reported precision at 60 and estimated recall weekly to the fraud lead, and after three months used the new labels to train a gradient boosting classifier on top of the anomaly scores.

lessons: Set the threshold from the review budget, then measure precision at that budget.
Context matters: compare each merchant with itself at that hour, not with every merchant at once.
Labels from reviewed alerts are the path from unsupervised scores to a supervised model.
Sample unflagged cases, or you will never learn what the system misses.

timeseries.title: Brindlecroft Bakeries: cutting bread waste with a forecast that beat 'last Saturday'
timeseries.company: Brindlecroft Bakeries (made up), chain of 38 bakery shops, about 400 staff, Ireland
timeseries.situation: Each shop manager ordered next week's bake by copying the same weekday from last week and adding a bit 'to be safe'. About 14 percent of baked goods were thrown away, and popular items still sold out by early afternoon on Saturdays. Head office asked for 'an AI demand forecast'.
timeseries.problem: A vendor demo had shown a neural network with '4 percent MAPE', but it had been tested on a random shuffle of days, excluded zero-sales items and was scored on the chain total, not per shop and item. Nobody knew whether it beat what managers already did.
approach: Defined the job with operations: a forecast per shop and product for each day of next week, made on Sunday evening, so the horizon is 1 to 7 days and only data up to Sunday may be used.
Rebuilt the managers' method as a seasonal-naive baseline and scored it with WAPE per shop and product, since MAPE was infinite on the many zero-sales days for slow items.
Set up a rolling backtest over 12 weekly folds covering Christmas and a bank holiday, training only on data before each Sunday.

Compared Holt-Winters per series with one gradient boosting model across all shops and products, using lags of 7 days or more, rolling means, day of week, school holidays and a weather forecast feature.
Found that boosting beat seasonal naive clearly on busy items and not on slow ones, so used boosting for the top 60 products and seasonal naive for the rest.
Sent the forecast to managers as a suggested order they could edit, and logged their edits to learn where the model was missing local knowledge.

timeseries.outcome: Over the first 10 weeks after launch, waste fell from about 14 percent to about 10 percent of baked goods, and Saturday sell-outs before 2pm fell by roughly a third. The hybrid's live WAPE stayed within 1.5 points of its backtest score.
lessons: Rebuild what people already do as a baseline; that is the bar the customer actually cares about.
Fix the horizon and the level first, then backtest on time-ordered folds that include hard periods.
Pick metrics that survive zeros; WAPE told the truth where MAPE could not.
Using different methods for different parts of the catalogue is fine if the backtest supports it.
discuss: How would you respond if the vendor insisted their 4 percent MAPE proved their model was better?
Manager edits improve the order but also change what gets sold. How could that bias future training data?
A new shop opens with no sales history. How would you forecast its orders for the first eight weeks?

recsys.title: Fennick Outdoor: proving a recommender earns its place on the product page
recsys.company: Fennick Outdoor (made up), online outdoor gear retailer, about 180 staff and 12,000 products, Canada
recsys.situation: Fennick's product pages showed 'Customers also viewed', filled by a hand-maintained list for the top 500 products and bestsellers everywhere else. About 4.1 percent of sessions that viewed a product page added a recommended item to the cart. The ecommerce director wanted 'AI recommendations' before the spring season.
recsys.problem: The team had no ratings, only views, add-to-carts and purchases, and 30 percent of the catalogue changed each season, so many products had no history. A prototype matrix factorization model looked impressive in a demo, but nobody had compared it with the existing bestseller logic.
approach: Rebuilt the current behaviour as a baseline: recent bestsellers within the product's category, filtered for items already in the cart or out of stock.
Built item-based collaborative filtering from co-purchases and add-to-carts, weighting purchases 3 times a view, and never treating unviewed items as negatives.
Added content-based candidates from product text embeddings for items under 45 days old, so new-season gear could appear on day one.
Evaluated offline on a time split (train to 1 February, test on the next four weeks) with precision@10, recall@10, NDCG@10 and catalogue coverage.
Designed a four-week A/B test with 50 percent of product-page traffic, add-to-cart rate from recommendations as the primary metric, and return rate and page load time as guardrails.

artifact.code:
A/B test plan: product-page recommendations

Hypothesis: hybrid CF + content recommendations raise add-to-cart
            from the widget versus category bestsellers.
Units:      visitors (sticky assignment by visitor id)
Split:      50% control (bestsellers) / 50% treatment (hybrid)
Primary:    add-to-cart rate from the widget per product-page session
Guardrails: return rate of widget-added items; p95 page load time
Min run:    4 full weeks (covers weekly cycle and a payday)
Sample:     about 300,000 sessions per arm to detect +0.4 points
Ship if:    primary improves and is significant at 95%, guardrails
            not worse by more than 0.5 points / 50 ms
No peeking: decision only at the end of week 4

recsys.outcome: Offline, the hybrid beat the baseline on NDCG@10 (0.21 versus 0.15) and tripled catalogue coverage. In the A/B test, add-to-cart from the widget rose from 4.1 to 4.8 percent with no change in returns or page speed, and the hybrid was rolled out to all traffic.
lessons: Rebuild what the site already does as the baseline, and beat it offline before any A/B test.
With implicit feedback, weight strong signals more and never treat unseen items as dislikes.
Plan cold start from day one when the catalogue changes every season.
Offline metrics pick candidates; an A/B test with guardrails decides what ships.

How would you stop the recommender from only ever showing already-popular products?
The A/B test ran for four weeks in autumn. Why might the result not hold in the summer season, and how would you check?
